items.explanation: The Radicals backed military rule, Johnson's impeachment, and Black officeholding — but they sought to bar ex-Confederate leaders from power, not restore them.
options: A. Military governance of the South
B. The impeachment of Andrew Johnson
C. Restoring ex-Confederate leaders to power
D. Electing newly enfranchised Black legislators
items.stem: Radical Republicans favored all of the following EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: The Radical Republicans did favor this: the Reconstruction Acts of 1867 divided the defeated South into five military districts governed by federal generals. Since the question asks which item they did NOT favor, military governance cannot be the answer.
option_explanations.B: Radical Republicans drove Johnson's impeachment — Thaddeus Stevens and the House Radicals led the 1868 effort. They favored it, so it is not the exception the question asks for.
option_explanations.C: This is the exception the question asks for, so it is correct. The Radicals wanted ex-Confederate leaders kept out of power — through loyalty oaths, the Fourteenth Amendment's disqualification of those who had sworn oaths and then rebelled, and support for newly enfranchised Black voters. Restoring the old Southern leadership to power was Andrew Johnson's approach, not the Radicals'.
option_explanations.D: The Radicals championed Black suffrage and celebrated Black officeholders like Bruce; supporting Black legislators was central to their program, so this cannot be the exception.

items.explanation: The House impeached Johnson for firing Secretary of War Stanton in defiance of the Tenure of Office Act — though the real clash was over his lenient Reconstruction policies.
options: A. Violating the Tenure of Office Act
B. Violating the Reconstruction Act
C. Pursuing too lenient a Southern policy
D. Failing to enforce the Civil Rights Act of 1866
items.stem: The stated legal ground for Andrew Johnson's impeachment was

option_explanations.A: Correct. The House's articles of impeachment charged Johnson with violating the Tenure of Office Act by removing Secretary of War Edwin Stanton without Senate approval. That statute was the stated legal basis, even though the deeper cause was Johnson's obstruction of Reconstruction.
option_explanations.B: Johnson clashed bitterly with Congress over the Reconstruction Acts, but violating them was never the charge — the articles of impeachment named the Tenure of Office Act, not the Reconstruction Acts.
option_explanations.C: Johnson's lenient Southern policy was the real political reason the Radicals wanted him gone, but it was not the stated legal ground of the impeachment articles — Congress needed a statutory violation, and it chose the Tenure of Office Act.
option_explanations.D: Johnson vetoed the Civil Rights Act of 1866 (Congress overrode the veto), but failure to enforce it was not an article of impeachment; the charge was the Stanton firing under the Tenure of Office Act.

items.explanation: Southern legislatures in 1865–66 passed Black Codes restricting Black movement, barring them from most occupations, and binding them to plantation labor — slavery in all but name.
options: A. To expand Black political participation
B. To strengthen the Freedmen's Bureau
C. To bar Black workers from many occupations
D. To preserve slavery in the Deep South

option_explanations.A: The opposite of what happened. Black Codes were designed to restrict Black political and economic life, not expand it — Black political participation came through federal action like the Reconstruction Acts and the Fifteenth Amendment, not through the codes.
option_explanations.B: Black Codes had nothing to do with the Freedmen's Bureau, a federal agency created to aid formerly enslaved people with food, schooling, and labor contracts. The codes were state laws meant to control Black labor, which the Bureau often tried to counteract.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Southern legislatures in 1865–66 passed Black Codes that barred Black people from most occupations, restricted their movement, and bound them to plantation labor through harsh vagrancy and apprenticeship laws — a system critics called slavery in all but name.
option_explanations.D: Slavery itself had already been abolished by the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865, so there was no slavery left to 'preserve.' The Black Codes were the South's attempt to recreate its substance — forced, cheap Black labor — under a new legal form.

items.explanation: The 1877 bargain gave Hayes the presidency in exchange for withdrawing the last federal troops from the South, ending Reconstruction and abandoning Black Southerners to white rule.
options: A. A presidential order ended it
B. Federal troops were withdrawn from the South
C. Hayes personally opposed Reconstruction
D. Black political power made it unnecessary
items.stem: Reconstruction ended with the Compromise of 1877 because

option_explanations.A: No presidential order ended Reconstruction. It ended through the political bargain of the Compromise of 1877 — an informal congressional deal, not an executive decree.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Compromise of 1877 settled the disputed 1876 election: Democrats accepted Republican Rutherford B. Hayes as president, and in return the last federal troops were withdrawn from Louisiana and South Carolina. Without troops to protect Black voters and Republican state governments, Reconstruction collapsed.
option_explanations.C: Hayes was a Republican, and personal opposition was not the cause. He accepted the troop-withdrawal bargain as the price of the presidency; the end of Reconstruction came from the deal itself, not from his personal views.
option_explanations.D: The opposite of reality. By 1877 Black political power was being destroyed — federal protection was removed precisely so Southern Democrats could reclaim power and strip Black citizens of their rights. If Black political power had been secure, Reconstruction would not have needed to end.

items.explanation: Ratified in 1870, the Fifteenth Amendment barred denying the vote 'on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.'
options: A. Readmitted Southern states to the Union
B. Abolished slavery
C. Barred racial discrimination in voting
D. Disqualified ex-Confederate officials from office

option_explanations.A: Readmission of Southern states to the Union was a political process governed by Congress's Reconstruction requirements (including ratifying the Fourteenth Amendment), not by the Fifteenth Amendment.
option_explanations.B: Slavery was abolished by the Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in 1865 — five years before the Fifteenth Amendment.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Ratified in 1870, the Fifteenth Amendment provided that the right to vote could not be denied 'on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude' — a bar on racial discrimination in voting.
option_explanations.D: Disqualifying ex-Confederate officials from office came from Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment, not the Fifteenth. The Fifteenth dealt only with voting rights.

items.explanation: Bruce spoke in March 1876 -- the very year the disputed presidential election would produce the Compromise of 1877 and the withdrawal of the last federal troops from the South. Within a few years, Mississippi's Black voters were being driven from the polls and Bruce's optimism buried under Jim Crow. The date marks Reconstruction's collapse, not its triumph.
options: A. Slavery had just been abolished the year before
B. Federal protection of Black rights was collapsing as Reconstruction ended
C. The modern civil rights movement was at its peak
D. The New Deal was beginning to aid Black Southerners
items.stem: Bruce delivered this optimistic speech in 1876 -- a date significant because
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"I have confidence, not only in this country and her institutions, but in the endurance, capacity, and destiny of my people. We will, as opportunities arise, continue to prove ourselves worthy of the responsibilities that citizenship imposes."
—Senator Blanche K. Bruce (R-MS), speech in the U.S. Senate, 1870s (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Wrong era by a decade: slavery was abolished in 1865 with the Thirteenth Amendment, not the year before 1876. Bruce's speech came eleven years after emancipation.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Bruce spoke in March 1876 — the very year the disputed presidential election would produce the Compromise of 1877 and the withdrawal of the last federal troops from the South. His optimism was voiced just as federal protection of Black rights was collapsing.
option_explanations.C: Off by about ninety years. The modern civil rights movement peaked in the 1950s and 1960s — long after Bruce's death in 1898 and Reconstruction's end.
option_explanations.D: Off by about sixty years. The New Deal began in 1933 under Franklin Roosevelt; in 1876 the federal government was abandoning the South, not beginning to aid Black Southerners.

items.explanation: Black Southerners voted overwhelmingly Republican — the party of Lincoln, emancipation, and Reconstruction.
options: A. Democratic
B. Republican
C. Populist
D. Greenback
items.stem: As an African American officeholder of his era, Bruce was almost certainly a

option_explanations.A: In the Reconstruction-era South, the Democratic Party was the party of white supremacy and the architects of Black Codes and later Jim Crow. Black voters overwhelmingly rejected it, not joined it.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Black Southerners voted overwhelmingly Republican — the party of Lincoln, emancipation, and Reconstruction. Every Black Reconstruction-era senator and congressman, Bruce included, was a Republican.
option_explanations.C: The Populist movement did not exist in 1876. The People's Party emerged in the 1890s, a decade after Bruce left the Senate in 1881 — it could not have been his party.
option_explanations.D: The Greenback Party was a small 1870s–80s third party focused on currency reform. Black Southern voters put their political weight behind the Republicans, who had freed them, not behind a currency-focused third party.

items.explanation: Bruce's counsel of patience -- Black Southerners proving their worthiness through labor and self-improvement, 'cultivators of the soil' -- parallels Washington's Atlanta Compromise. Du Bois would soon break with exactly this program, demanding the vote, enforcement of civil rights, and higher education now, not after some probationary period of good behavior.
options: A. W. E. B. Du Bois's demand for immediate civil rights and higher education
B. Booker T. Washington's Atlanta Compromise
C. Southern sharecroppers' desire for land of their own
D. Abraham Lincoln's emancipation policy
items.stem: Bruce's emphasis on patience and self-improvement differed most sharply from
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"I have confidence, not only in this country and her institutions, but in the endurance, capacity, and destiny of my people. We will, as opportunities arise, continue to prove ourselves worthy of the responsibilities that citizenship imposes."
—Senator Blanche K. Bruce (R-MS), speech in the U.S. Senate, 1870s (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Correct — this is the sharpest contrast. Du Bois would soon demand the vote, enforcement of civil rights, and higher education for Black Americans immediately, directly rejecting the gradualist counsel of patience and self-improvement through labor that Bruce voiced here.
option_explanations.B: Not the sharpest contrast — Washington's 1895 Atlanta Compromise preached the same philosophy Bruce voices here: economic self-improvement and patience before demanding full political equality. The two are parallel, not opposed.
option_explanations.C: Not the real contrast. Southern sharecroppers wanted land of their own, and Bruce's speech — urging Black people to be 'cultivators of the soil' — was aimed at exactly such working people. A landowner's argument differs in economics, not in the patience-versus-protest philosophy the question targets.
option_explanations.D: Lincoln's emancipation policy is what made Bruce's speech possible — emancipation freed Black people; Bruce's question is what freedpeople should do next. Lincoln's policy was an action, not a competing philosophy about gradualism versus protest, so it is not the sharpest contrast with Bruce's position.
